title: Correlation, Causation, and Sample Size
description: Master the critical distinctions between correlation and causation, and understand when sample sizes are large enough to trust.

interactions.prompt: A study finds cities with more ice cream shops have higher crime rates. What's the most likely explanation?

options.text: Ice cream causes criminal behavior
A confounding variable like population size drives both
Crime causes people to open ice cream shops
The data must be incorrect

interactions.teachingPreamble: Correlation means two variables move together, but it doesn't mean one causes the other. Often, a hidden third variable — called a confounding variable — drives both. For example, larger cities naturally have more of everything: more shops, more incidents, more people.

interactions.prompt: Spotify finds that users who create playlists have 3x higher retention. Playlist creators also skew 80% toward users aged 18-24. What's the key insight before acting on this data?

options.text: Immediately build features to push all users to create playlists
Age is a likely confound — younger users may retain better regardless
Playlist creation definitively causes higher retention
The 3x figure is too large to be a coincidence

interactions.prompt: Your startup tested a new checkout flow with 30 users and saw a 15% conversion lift. Should you roll it out company-wide?

options.text: Yes — 15% is a meaningful improvement worth shipping
No — 30 users is far too small to trust the result
Only if the 30 users were all power users
Yes, but reduce the lift estimate to 7.5% to be safe

interactions.teachingPreamble: Sample size determines how much you can trust a result. With small samples, random variation can easily produce dramatic but meaningless differences. A general rule: most A/B tests need hundreds or thousands of observations per variant to detect real effects reliably. Thirty users could swing wildly just by chance.

interactions.prompt: When a result is unlikely to have occurred by random chance alone, statisticians call it ____.

options.text: Statistically significant
Causally proven
Normally distributed
Positively correlated

interactions.prompt: Your CEO wants to launch a pricing change next week based on a survey of 50 customers showing strong demand. Your data team says a proper test needs 4 more weeks and 2,000 users. A competitor may move soon. What do you recommend?

options.text: Launch now — speed matters more than perfect data
Run the full test — a bad pricing decision is very costly
Soft-launch to 10% of users as a compromise
Survey 200 more customers this week for faster signal

interactions.prompt: Netflix observes that users who rate 20+ movies churn less. They design a campaign nudging all users to rate more movies, but churn doesn't improve. Why?

options.text: The campaign probably didn't reach enough users
Rating movies doesn't cause retention — engaged users just do both
Users rated the wrong types of movies
Churn is too complex to be influenced by any single action

interactions.teachingPreamble: This is the correlation-causation trap in action at scale. When companies observe that power users do X, they assume making all users do X will create power users. But the behavior is often a symptom of engagement, not its cause. The underlying trait — genuine interest — drives both the behavior and the outcome.

interactions.prompt: Rank these findings from MOST to LEAST trustworthy for making a business decision: (a) Survey of 40 customers shows 80% want a feature, (b) 10,000-user A/B test shows 4% conversion lift at p<0.05, (c) Industry report correlating social media spend with revenue, (d) Internal analysis of 500 customers controlling for confounders.

options.text: Survey of 40 customers, 80% want a feature
10,000-user A/B test, 4% lift, statistically significant
Industry report correlating spend with revenue
Internal analysis of 500 customers, confounders controlled

interactions.prompt: You ran that 10,000-user A/B test and got a statistically significant 4% lift. But now you discover 60% of the test group were mobile users while only 35% of the control group were. Is your result still trustworthy?

options.text: Yes — 10,000 users is large enough to overcome any imbalance
No — the uneven mobile split is a confound that invalidates the result
Only if mobile and desktop users convert at similar rates
Re-run the test but exclude all mobile users entirely

interactions.priorContext: Previously you ranked a 10,000-user A/B test as the most trustworthy evidence. Now new information reveals the test and control groups weren't balanced — the test group was disproportionately mobile users, introducing a potential confounding variable that could explain the lift.
